claims.text: Service-relevant thermal and mechanical loading can induce dynamic nanosegregation in initially single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Ni, Cr, and Mn preferentially form separate nanoclusters at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary enrichment by these principal elements reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes crack initiation and brittle intergranular fracture.
The proposed embrittlement can occur without conventional intermetallic precipitation.
The starting material is an equiaxed, compositionally complex, single-phase solid solution that is initially uniform and free of grain-boundary precipitates.
Changing cooling conditions can promote or inhibit grain-boundary atomic mobility and segregation during subsequent tensile deformation.
Intermediate-temperature tensile deformation is an appropriate regime in which to test segregation-associated ductility loss.
Atomic redistribution can be active over the stated range from room temperature to moderately high temperature when strain rates provide sufficient time.
Inherent lattice distortion and high configurational entropy drive element-specific grain-boundary segregation.
Nanoclustering changes local grain-boundary chemistry and bonding, creating weak sites for crack nucleation.
Conditions favoring segregation should produce earlier intergranular cracking and lower ductility than conditions suppressing segregation.
Suppressing grain-boundary segregation should preserve higher toughness despite a similar overall microstructure.
Modified cooling rates or minor additions of segregation-inhibiting alloying elements can suppress grain-boundary segregation.
Conventional-alloy brittleness arises primarily from grain-boundary precipitation and rapid grain coarsening.
In single-phase HEAs without classical precipitates, brittle behavior is not expected unless dynamic segregation occurs.
The mechanism is limited to temperatures and deformation conditions that permit segregation but do not cause intermetallic formation or substantial grain coarsening.
The critical temperatures, strain rates, segregation kinetics, and composition sensitivities have not yet been quantified.
A verified reduction in segregation that fails to improve ductility or delay intergranular cracking would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.

contradictions.description: The experiment is framed as a comparison of single-phase HEAs with similar microstructures, but one proposed suppression route uses minor alloying and the cited demonstrated route redirects segregation into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. Such interventions may change composition or phase constitution rather than isolate grain-boundary segregation.
